options: Hopeful, with some sadness at leaving
questions.why: They are sorry to leave, but hopeful about Glinda.

questions.q: What do Dorothy, the Lion and Toto do while the Tin Woodman builds the ladder?
questions.why: They are tired from the long walk.

questions.q: What does the Scarecrow say he can't figure out?
options: Why the wall is there, or what it's made of
questions.why: The Tin Woodman tells him to rest his brains, since they'll know once they climb over.

questions.q: Who climbs the ladder first?
questions.why: When he looks over the top, he says, 'Oh, my!'

questions.q: What does each traveler say on seeing over the wall?
questions.why: Everyone is amazed by the view.

questions.q: What is the floor of the China Country like?
options: As smooth, shining and white as the bottom of a big platter
questions.why: The whole country looks like fine dishware.

questions.q: How big are the houses in the China Country?
options: The biggest are only as high as Dorothy's waist
questions.why: Everything here is small and delicate.

questions.q: How do the travelers get down from the wall?
options: The Scarecrow jumps down first, and the others jump onto him so the hard floor won't hurt their feet
questions.why: They are careful not to land on his head and get pins in their feet.

questions.q: Why do they have to cross the China Country instead of going around?
options: It would be unwise to go any way except due South
questions.why: Their goal, Glinda's castle, lies to the south.

questions.q: What happens when the travelers startle the china cow?
options: It kicks over the stool, the pail and the milkmaid, and breaks its own leg
It turns into a real cow
questions.why: The pail breaks into pieces, and the milkmaid's elbow gets nicked.

questions.q: Where does the milkmaid say she must take her cow?
options: To the mender's shop, to have the leg glued on
questions.why: In this country, broken things are glued back together.

questions.q: How does Dorothy respond to the angry milkmaid?
options: She says she's very sorry and asks her to forgive them
questions.why: Dorothy is polite even when others are rude to her.

questions.q: What lesson does Dorothy take from the milkmaid?
options: They must be very careful, or they may hurt these little people in ways that can't be undone
questions.why: The China Country is a place where being clumsy has real costs.

questions.q: Why won't the china Princess run?
options: If she runs she may fall down and break herself
questions.why: Being delicate limits everything she does.

questions.q: What does the Princess say about being mended?
options: One is never so pretty after being mended
questions.why: Repairs are possible, but they leave marks.

questions.q: Who is Mr. Joker?
options: A clown who has broken himself so often, standing on his head, that he's mended in a hundred places
questions.why: His cracks run in every direction.

questions.q: What is Mr. Joker always trying to do?
questions.why: That's how he keeps breaking himself.

questions.q: What does Dorothy want to do with the Princess?
options: Take her to Kansas and stand her on Aunt Em's mantel
questions.why: Dorothy means it kindly — she admires the Princess.

questions.q: Why does the Princess say being taken away would make her unhappy?
options: Away from her own country, her joints would stiffen, and she could only stand straight and look pretty
questions.why: At home she can talk and move as she pleases.

questions.q: How do the travelers get over the second china wall?
options: They climb up on the Lion's back to reach the top, and then the Lion jumps up
They break a hole in it
questions.why: The second wall is not as high as the first.

questions.q: What does the Lion accidentally break as he jumps?
options: A china church, with his tail
questions.why: Dorothy thinks they were lucky to do no more harm than a cow's leg and a church.

chapters.title: 21. The Lion Becomes the King of Beasts

questions.q: What is the land like after the china wall?
options: Bogs and marshes covered with tall, rank grass, with hidden muddy holes
questions.why: The land is hard to walk through without falling into muddy holes.

questions.q: When Dorothy wonders whether wild beasts live in the forest, what does the Lion say?
options: He supposes there are, but he doesn't see any about
questions.why: He is too pleased with the forest to worry.

questions.q: What kind of forest do the travelers enter?
options: A forest with trees bigger and older than any they have seen
questions.why: It is a wild, ancient place.

questions.q: How does the Lion feel about this forest?
options: He wants to leave at once
He says it is perfectly delightful and he'd like to live there all his life
questions.why: He loves the soft dried leaves and the rich green moss.

questions.q: How does the Scarecrow feel about the forest?
questions.why: Each friend sees the same place differently.

questions.q: Who keeps watch overnight in the forest?
options: The Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow
questions.why: Dorothy, Toto and the Lion sleep while the two who never tire stand guard.

questions.q: What do the travelers find in the morning?
options: Hundreds of beasts holding a meeting
questions.why: Tigers, elephants, bears, wolves and foxes have gathered, and they seem to be in great trouble.

questions.q: What happens when the beasts see the Lion?
options: The whole crowd goes quiet at once
questions.why: They recognize a lion as a great king.

questions.q: Who speaks for the animals?
questions.why: He bows and welcomes the Lion as King of Beasts.

questions.q: What is the monster like?
options: Like a great spider, with a body as big as an elephant and eight legs as long as tree trunks
questions.why: It grabs animals with its legs and drags them to its mouth, as a spider does a fly.

questions.q: What happened to the other lions in the forest?
questions.why: The tiger adds that none of them were as big and brave as this Lion.

questions.q: What does the Lion ask in return for fighting the monster?
options: That the beasts bow down to him and obey him as King of the Forest
questions.why: The beasts agree gladly.

questions.q: What does the Lion do before going to fight?
options: Asks the beasts to take good care of his friends
Asks the Tin Woodman to come
questions.why: He marches off proudly to fight alone.

questions.q: What is the monster doing when the Lion finds it?
questions.why: The Lion knows it's better to fight it asleep than awake.

questions.q: What is the monster's weak point?
options: Its head is joined to its body by a neck as slender as a wasp's waist
questions.why: The Lion sees this and uses it.

questions.q: How does the Lion defeat the monster?
options: He tricks it into the river
He springs onto its back and knocks its head off with one blow of his clawed paw
questions.why: He plans his attack carefully, and it works.

questions.q: What does the Lion tell the beasts after the fight?
options: That they need fear their enemy no longer
That they must fight next time
questions.why: They bow down to him as their King.

questions.q: What does the Lion promise the beasts?
options: To stay with them forever right away
To come back and rule them once Dorothy is safely on her way to Kansas
questions.why: He keeps his promise to Dorothy first.

questions.q: How has the Lion changed since Chapter 6?
options: Once ashamed of his cowardice, he now faces a monster alone and becomes King of Beasts
questions.why: His courage has grown — or he has finally recognized it.

questions.q: Why does it matter that the Lion puts Dorothy first?
options: It shows he is still afraid
It shows he doesn't want to be king
It shows he doesn't trust the animals
It shows loyalty to his friend over his own reward
questions.why: Friendship comes before the crown.

questions.q: What blocks the travelers after the forest?
options: A steep hill covered from top to bottom with great pieces of rock
questions.why: The Scarecrow says it will be a hard climb, but they must get over it.

questions.q: What does a voice cry as the Scarecrow nears the first rock?
questions.why: The speaker says the hill belongs to his people and no one may cross.

questions.q: What is strange about the man who steps out?
options: He is short and stout, with a big head flat on top, a thick wrinkled neck, and no arms at all
questions.why: Because he has no arms, the Scarecrow thinks he is helpless.

questions.q: How does the Hammer-Head knock down the Scarecrow?
options: His head shoots forward on a stretching neck and strikes the Scarecrow
questions.why: The head then snaps back to his body.

questions.q: What happens when the Lion charges up the hill?
options: A head shoots out, and the Lion rolls down the hill as if struck by a cannon ball
He is caught in a net
questions.why: The Lion is bruised and sore.

questions.q: Why does the Lion get angry?
options: The Hammer-Heads laugh at the Scarecrow's fall
questions.why: Hundreds of Hammer-Heads laugh from behind the rocks.

questions.q: How many Hammer-Heads are on the hill?
questions.why: The first man wasn't alone at all.

questions.q: What does the Lion conclude after being knocked down?
options: It's useless to fight people with shooting heads
questions.why: Strength alone won't work here.

questions.q: Who suggests calling the Winged Monkeys?
questions.why: He reminds Dorothy she still has the right to command them once more.

questions.q: What does Dorothy command the Monkeys to do?
options: Carry them over the hill to the country of the Quadlings
Take them to the Emerald City
questions.why: This is her third and last call.

questions.q: How do the Hammer-Heads react as the Monkeys fly over?
options: They yell with vexation and shoot their heads high in the air, but can't reach
questions.why: The travelers are out of reach.

questions.q: What does the Monkey King say when he sets them down?
options: "This is the last time you can summon us, so good-bye and good luck"
questions.why: Dorothy's three calls are now used up.

questions.q: What color is everything in the Quadling Country?
questions.why: Just as the Winkies' land is yellow and the Munchkins' blue.

questions.q: What are the Quadlings like?
options: Short and fat, chubby and good-natured, dressed all in red
questions.why: Their red clothes stand out against the green grass.

questions.q: What does the Quadling Country look like?
options: A rich, happy land with field upon field of ripening grain, good roads and strong bridges
questions.why: It's one of the most peaceful places they visit.

questions.q: Who feeds the travelers?
questions.why: She gives them a good dinner, with cakes and cookies, and a bowl of milk for Toto.

questions.q: What does the farmer's wife say about Glinda's castle?
options: It isn't far — take the road to the South
questions.why: They set off again feeling hopeful.

questions.q: Who guards the gates of Glinda's castle?
options: Three young girls in handsome red uniforms trimmed with gold braid
questions.why: One of them takes Dorothy's name to Glinda.

questions.q: What happens after the girl soldier brings Dorothy's name to Glinda?
options: They are to be let in at once
questions.why: Unlike Oz, Glinda sees them right away.

questions.q: How is Glinda's welcome different from Oz's?
options: Glinda lets them in at once, while Oz kept them waiting and gave them a dangerous task
questions.why: The contrast hints at the difference between real goodness and pretending.

chapters.title: 23. Glinda The Good Witch Grants Dorothy's Wish

questions.q: How do the travelers get ready before meeting Glinda?
options: Dorothy washes and combs her hair, the Lion shakes the dust from his mane, the Scarecrow pats himself into shape, and the Woodman polishes and oils himself
questions.why: They want to look their best for the Good Witch.

questions.q: What is Glinda's throne made of?
questions.why: Red is the color of the South.

questions.q: How does Glinda look?
options: Beautiful and young, with rich red hair, blue eyes and a pure white dress
questions.why: She looks kindly on Dorothy.

questions.q: What reason does Dorothy give for wanting to get home?
options: Aunt Em will surely think something dreadful has happened to her
questions.why: Dorothy thinks of others' feelings, even Aunt Em's worry — and of whether Uncle Henry can afford for Aunt Em to go into mourning.

questions.q: What does Glinda ask for in exchange for helping Dorothy?
questions.why: Dorothy gives it gladly, since it's no use to her now.

questions.q: How many commands will Glinda get from the Golden Cap?
questions.why: Glinda smiles and says she'll need the Monkeys exactly three times.

questions.q: What does the Scarecrow plan to do after Dorothy leaves?
options: Return to rule the Emerald City
questions.why: His only worry is crossing the hill of the Hammer-Heads.

questions.q: When the Scarecrow asks, 'Am I really wonderful?', what does Glinda answer?
questions.why: It's a gentle, funny, honest answer.

questions.q: Where does the Tin Woodman want to go?
options: To the land of the Winkies, to rule them
questions.why: The Winkies were kind to him and asked him to rule.

questions.q: What does Glinda say about the Tin Woodman's brains?
options: His brain may not look as large as the Scarecrow's, but he is really brighter — when well polished
He should ask Oz for some
questions.why: Another gentle joke — 'brighter' means both shinier and smarter.

questions.q: Where does the Lion want to go?
options: To the grand old forest where the beasts made him King
questions.why: Glinda's third command will carry him there.

questions.q: What will Glinda do with the Golden Cap after her three commands?
options: Give it to the Monkey King, so the Monkeys will be free forevermore
questions.why: Glinda uses her power to free others.

questions.q: What does Glinda reveal about the silver shoes?
options: They can carry Dorothy over the desert
questions.why: Dorothy had the way home all along.

questions.q: What does Glinda say Dorothy could have done on her very first day in Oz?
options: Gone back to Aunt Em, if she had known the shoes' power
questions.why: The answer was on her feet from the start.

questions.q: What does the Scarecrow say he would have missed if Dorothy had gone home the first day?
options: His wonderful brains — he might have spent his whole life in the cornfield
questions.why: The journey mattered as much as the destination.

questions.q: What does the Lion say he would have missed?
options: He would have lived a coward forever
questions.why: Each friend grew because of the journey.

questions.q: How do the silver shoes work?
options: Knock the heels together three times and command the shoes to carry you wherever you wish
Take them off and throw them
questions.why: Glinda says they can carry you anywhere in the world in three steps.

questions.q: How does Dorothy say goodbye to the Scarecrow?
options: She hugs his soft, stuffed body instead of kissing his painted face
questions.why: She finds she is crying at the parting.

questions.q: What does Dorothy say as she clicks her heels together?
questions.why: Her command names the person she has been longing for.

questions.q: What happens to the silver shoes on Dorothy's trip home?
options: They fall off during her flight and are lost forever in the desert
questions.why: Dorothy arrives in Kansas in her stocking-feet.

questions.q: What is Aunt Em doing when she sees Dorothy?
options: Coming out of the house to water the cabbages
questions.why: It is an ordinary moment on the farm.

questions.q: What does Dorothy do when Aunt Em sees her?
questions.why: Dorothy runs to Aunt Em.

questions.q: How does Aunt Em greet Dorothy?
options: She scolds her for being gone
She calls her 'my darling child,' holds her in her arms, and covers her face with kisses
questions.why: Aunt Em, once so gray and joyless, is overcome with love.

questions.q: What question does Aunt Em ask Dorothy?
options: "Where in the world did you come from?"
questions.why: She has no idea where Dorothy has been.

questions.q: How does Dorothy answer?
questions.why: She says it gravely, meaning it seriously.

questions.q: What does 'gravely' mean in "said Dorothy gravely"?
questions.why: She speaks with great seriousness about her adventure.

questions.q: Who else does Dorothy mention in her reply?
questions.why: "And here is Toto, too."

questions.q: What are Dorothy's last words in the book?
options: "Oh, Aunt Em! I'm so glad to be at home again!"
questions.why: The book ends where Dorothy's wish began: at home.

questions.q: How does Aunt Em's greeting differ from how she was described in Chapter 1?
options: She is warm and loving, not stern and gray
questions.why: Dorothy's return brings joy into the gray farmhouse.

questions.q: What central idea does this chapter complete?
options: There is no place like home
questions.why: Dorothy's longing for home, first spoken to the Scarecrow, is fulfilled.

questions.q: Why do you think this chapter is so short?
options: The author ran out of time
The joy of arriving home needs few words after the long journey
questions.why: A short, simple ending shows how complete Dorothy's happiness is.

questions.q: Which chapter first sets up the wish this chapter fulfills?
options: Chapter 2, when Dorothy first asks how to get back to Kansas
questions.why: From the moment she lands in Oz, Dorothy wants to go home.

questions.q: How did Dorothy arrive just before this scene?
options: By the silver shoes, whirling through the air from Glinda's castle
questions.why: Glinda showed her the shoes' power in Chapter 23.

questions.q: Who is with Dorothy at the end?
questions.why: Toto has been with her from the cyclone to the end.

questions.q: What has Dorothy gained from her journey, as the ending suggests?
options: A deeper sense of how much home and family matter to her
questions.why: She comes home glad and grateful.

questions.q: How does the tone of this ending feel?
questions.why: The reunion is loving and happy.

questions.q: What does Dorothy's return show about Aunt Em's feelings for her?
options: Aunt Em didn't notice she was gone
Aunt Em wanted her to stay away
questions.why: Her hugs and kisses show deep love.

questions.q: How is this final scene different from the colorful lands of Oz?
options: It's an ordinary farm scene — cabbages and a plain farmhouse — yet it is where Dorothy is happiest
questions.why: The book suggests that the plain, familiar place is worth more than all the wonders.

questions.q: Which friend first heard Dorothy say there was no place like home?
questions.why: In Chapter 4, the Scarecrow couldn't understand why she'd leave Oz for Kansas.

questions.q: What does Dorothy's joy at home prove about the Scarecrow's early confusion?
options: He was right that Oz is better
Home is valued for love and belonging, which beauty can't replace
questions.why: What Dorothy told the Scarecrow early on turns out to be true.

verdicts.high: There's no place like home — and no reader like you. Outstanding!
verdicts.pass: Well done. Follow the yellow brick road to the next chapter.
verdicts.fail: Below the passing mark. Reread the chapter and try again — courage means facing it when it's hard.

questions.q: What carries Dorothy from Kansas to Oz?
questions.why: The cyclone lifts her whole house and sets it down on the Wicked Witch of the East.

questions.q: What were the silver shoes able to do all along?
options: Carry her anywhere in three steps, including home across the desert
questions.why: Glinda reveals that Dorothy could have gone home on her first day.

questions.q: What does each of Dorothy's three companions want from Oz?
options: A home, a crown, a map
Wings, a voice, and a name
questions.why: The Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart, and the Lion courage.

questions.q: Which best states the book's idea about the friends' wishes?
options: Only magic can give people good qualities
The friends already showed the qualities they thought they lacked
questions.why: The Scarecrow plans, the Woodman cares, and the Lion faces danger long before Oz's 'gifts.'

questions.q: How is the Wicked Witch of the West destroyed?
options: Dorothy throws a bucket of water on her
questions.why: Dorothy acted in anger, with no idea water would melt her.

questions.q: Why does everything in the Emerald City look green?
questions.why: The Wizard admits the city is no greener than any other.

questions.q: Who is the Wizard, really?
options: A balloonist and ventriloquist from Omaha
questions.why: He says he is a very good man but a very bad Wizard.

questions.q: What limit does the Golden Cap have?
options: Each owner can call the Winged Monkeys only three times
It can be used only in the West
questions.why: Dorothy uses hers to reach the Emerald City, to ask to be carried to Kansas, and to cross the Hammer-Heads' hill.

questions.q: Which of these did Dorothy NOT use the Golden Cap for?
options: Asking to be carried to Kansas
Crossing the hill of the Hammer-Heads
questions.why: Water destroyed the Witch; the cap had nothing to do with it.

questions.q: Which pair of witches is good?
questions.why: The Witch of the North and Glinda of the South are good.

questions.q: Which color matches each people?
options: Munchkins red, Winkies blue, Quadlings yellow
Munchkins blue, Winkies yellow, Quadlings red
Munchkins green, Winkies red, Quadlings blue
Munchkins yellow, Winkies green, Quadlings blue
questions.why: Blue in the East, yellow in the West, red in the South, and green in the center.

questions.q: What protects Dorothy from the Winged Monkeys and the Wicked Witch?
options: The mark of the Good Witch of the North's kiss
questions.why: The Monkey King says the Power of Good is greater than the Power of Evil.

questions.q: What twice causes Dorothy to miss a way out?
questions.why: Toto sends her after him in the cyclone and again at the balloon launch.

questions.q: Who rescues the sleeping Lion from the poppy field?
options: The field mice, pulling a truck
questions.why: The Queen of the Field Mice repays the Tin Woodman for saving her.

questions.q: What does the Lion finally become?
options: King of the Beasts in a great forest
questions.why: He kills the spider-like monster and wins the forest's loyalty.

questions.q: Who ends up ruling the Emerald City and the Winkies?
options: The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman
questions.why: Glinda sends each friend where he wants to go.

questions.q: What does the Wizard tell the Lion about true courage?
options: It means facing danger even when you are afraid
questions.why: This is one of the book's central lessons.

questions.q: Why does Dorothy keep wanting to leave such a beautiful land?
options: There is no place like home, and she loves Aunt Em and Uncle Henry
questions.why: Home and family matter more than beauty or adventure.

questions.q: Which obstacle does the Tin Woodman's axe help the group get past?
options: The Kalidahs, by cutting the tree bridge
questions.why: He chops the tree so the Kalidahs fall into the gulf.

questions.q: What happens to the silver shoes in the end?
options: They fall off in the air and are lost forever in the desert
questions.why: Dorothy arrives in Kansas in her stocking-feet.

questions.q: How does the book show the value of small creatures?
options: The mice rescue the Lion, and little Toto exposes the Wizard
Small creatures are always in danger
questions.why: Some of the book's biggest turning points come from its smallest characters.

questions.q: What does Glinda do with the Golden Cap after using it?
options: Gives it to the Monkey King, setting the Monkeys free
questions.why: Real goodness uses power to free others.

questions.q: Which chapter titles are in the correct order?
options: The Cowardly Lion, The Deadly Poppy Field, The Guardian of the Gates
The Deadly Poppy Field, The Cowardly Lion, The Rescue
The Rescue, The Cyclone, Home Again
The Winged Monkeys, The Queen of the Field Mice, The Cyclone
questions.why: Chapters 6, 8 and 10 come in that order.

questions.q: How are the Wizard and Glinda different?
options: The Wizard pretends to have power, while Glinda has real power and uses it kindly
questions.why: The book contrasts false appearances with true goodness.

questions.q: Which details best show the book's idea that appearances can deceive?
options: The green spectacles and the Wizard's fake forms
questions.why: What looks grand and green turns out to be a trick of the eye.
